paper_title: Macaron-V1: Towards Open Continual Learning with Self-Improvement and Mixture-of-LoRA

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Macaron-V1 is an open agent-model family for experiential intelligence: learning from experience in real environments and continuing to learn after deployment. It is organized around two system goals. Adaptation is pursued through recursive improvement of versioned model-harness pairs, where experience from one configuration is evaluated under an external contract and used to construct its successor. Collaboration is pursued via the Mixture-of-LoRA (MoL) architecture that freezes a base model, composes specialist LoRA adapters, and selects one LoRA per user turn. The flagship Macaron-V1-Venti combines a 744B GLM-5.2 base with four LoRAs for chat, agent, coding, and GenUI; the Qwen3.6-based Macaron-V1-Tall (50B) uses the same design for local deployment. This report presents Macaron-V1 as a co-designed system spanning architecture, algorithms, and infrastructure. The MoL architecture supports continual learning through extensible LoRA specialists. The algorithm combines Model-Harness Co-design and recursive self-improvement loop, including the UI4A component-native GenUI harness, a stateful action substrate, versioned HCP contract, and the agentic RL framework MindForge. The supporting infrastructure includes the post-training platform MinT, the long-context RL method LongStraw, and stability techniques for sparse MoE and DSA base models. We evaluate Macaron-V1 on Personal Intelligence, GenUI, and general capability benchmarks against frontier baselines. Our results validate the current system, while compounding gains from continual learning and collective intelligence remain open questions.

sections.title: 3 Algorithm: Model–Harness Co-design and Recursive Self-Improvement
1 Introduction
sections.content: As pre-trained models mature, an increasing share of advances in capabilities such as agentic tool use and coding has come from post-training (OpenAI, 2026; Anthropic, 2026; Moonshot AI, 2025; GLM-5 Team, 2026). The effectiveness of post-training, however, is closely coupled to the environment in which model is trained, evaluated, and deployed (Yao, 2025; Lee et al., 2026b; Karten et al., 2026). The data model learns from, the tools it can use, the users it serves, and the interactions it must support jointly shape the behavior required of deployed agent (Harrington et al., 2026; Karten et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026b). These conditions vary across deployments and continue to evolve over time, as new knowledge becomes available, new domains emerge, and interaction state accumulates across episodes (Li et al., 2025a; Harrington et al., 2026; Jin et al., 2026). common practice is centralized post-training, in which model is optimized over bounded set of tasks and environments, aligned with the current harness, and consolidated into checkpoint for release. Training on broad task mixture can improve aggregate performance across tasks, but heterogeneous objectives can also create cross-task interference when they compete through shared parameters (Wang et al., 2026). More fundamentally, the resulting system remains tied to the task and environment distribution available during training, while new knowledge, tools, user needs, and interactions continue to arrive after release (Li et al., 2025a; Harrington et al., 2026; Karten et al., 2026; Jin et al., 2026). We see this as approximating static optimum rather than constituting genuine intelligence. What we consider genuine intelligence is experiential intelligence: the ability to learn from experience accumulated in real environment and to keep learning after deployment (Silver and Sutton, 2025; Yao, 2025). Mind Lab is built for experiential intelligence. We use Personal Intelligence for the user-facing competence required when an agent works over time for particular person: using tools reliably, remembering constraints across sessions, deciding when to ask clarifying question and when to act, and staying honest with the person on the other end of the conversation. These behaviors describe the product target; experiential intelligence adds temporal requirement that deployment experience feeds later modelharness revision. Current agentmodel training largely treats the target behaviors as capabilities to develop before release and then hold fixed: the model is tuned against snapshot of the environment and shipped. Once deployed, the resulting system has limited mechanisms for turning execution experience into systematic improvement over time (Jin et al., 2026; Karten et al., 2026). Macaron-V1 is our attempt to build that revision loop. Adaptation and collaboration. Experiential intelligence, as we operationalize it, has two complementary dimensions, and Macaron-V1 is built around both. Adaptation is pursued through recursive improvement over explicitly versioned modelharness pairs: each version names fixed model snapshot and runtime configuration. Recent approaches differ in where and how they make experience persistent. Parametric continual-learning methods update model weights across changing tasks or distributions (Chen et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2025a; Harrington et al., 2026). Memoryand state-based methods carry trajectories, retrieved experience, or compact online states forward without immediately modifying model parameters (Li et al., 2026b; Lei et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026c; Jin et al., 2026). Contextand harness-based methods instead update the instructions, tools, skills, memory procedures, orchestration, or execution structure surrounding the model (Zhang et al., 2026a; Lee et al., 2026b; Karten et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026a). Macaron-V1 connects harness adaptation with modular parametric adaptation: it builds harder tasks from seeds, audits trajectories in the production harness, searches the context configurations that shape behavior, and selects trajectories for subsequent updates to specialist LoRA adapters. Adaptation is therefore property we seek across successive modelharness revisions rather than in any single checkpoint. We use recursive improvement in bounded and auditable sense: experience generated by one versioned modelharness configuration is evaluated under an external contract and used to construct successor revision (Chen et al., 2026b). Repeating this process across successive revisions, while measuring retention, transfer, and cumulative improvement, is the longer-term continual-learning objective (Chen et al., 2026a; Harrington et al., 2026). Collaboration is pursued through composition. Joint post-training over heterogeneous tasks within shared 3 Figure 2 Three ways to scale model capability. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) scales the base itself; skills scale scaffolding around fixed model; MoL (Mixture of LoRA) keeps the base frozen and composes specialist LoRA adapters through Proxy-mediated routing loop. This separation is an implementation substrate for our continual-learning and collectiveintelligence goals; the diagram is not controlled comparison of the three alternatives. parameter space can create cross-task interference, motivating representation in which specialists remain separable (Wang et al., 2026). Existing approaches compose specialists at different granularities: mixtureof-adapter systems select or combine LoRA specialists at the task, sequence, or token level (Dhasade et al., 2026; Shah and Wagle, 2026), while multi-agent systems coordinate complete model instances through routing, communication, discussion, or response aggregation (Tran et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025b). Mixture-of-LoRA (MoL) occupies different operating point: it keeps large base model frozen, layers specialist LoRA adapters on top (Hu et al., 2022; Schulman and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025), and selects one specialist per user turn through shared runtime (Mind Lab, 2026d). MoL demonstrates modular collaboration. We reserve collective intelligence for the stronger setting in which independently trained specialists contribute complementary capabilities, enabling the composed system either to outperform its strongest constituent or to solve tasks that no constituent can solve alone under matched evaluation budget (Li et al., 2025b; Zhu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026a). Extending MoL to include specialists trained by different teams or for different users is the broader collective-intelligence objective. Adaptation and collaboration are complementary dimensions of an evolving agent system. Collaboration determines how distinct capabilities are represented, selected, and composed, while adaptation determines how those capabilities and the surrounding harness change in response to experience. Extending this process across multiple generations, so that specialists, routing policies, and harness configurations improve together while retaining prior capabilities, remains longer-term research direction (Huang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b). Model family. Macaron-V1 is family of open models rather than single checkpoint. Macaron-V1-Venti: the flagship release, conventionally labeled 748B, consisting of 744B GLM-5.2 base (Zhipu AI, 2026; GLM-5 Team, 2026) and four LoRA specialists. The label is release-facing; Section 2.2 4 gives the public stored-tensor count. It is post-trained with MinT (Lu et al., 2026) and served through the MoL harness (Mind Lab, 2026d). Macaron-V1-Tall: 50B model post-trained from Qwen3.6 (Qwen Team, 2026a, 2025), targeted at local deployment and lower-latency serving. It ships the same four-adapter MoL design as Macaron-V1-Venti, with adapter placement and ranks chosen for Qwen3.6s MoE expert layout. Its public adapter configurations use different rank and expert target set from Macaron-V1-Venti; the resulting aggregate is therefore reported as rounded release footprint rather than inferred from base size alone. Macaron-V1-Coding-Venti: coding-specialized build of Macaron-V1-Venti released by merging the coding LoRA directly into the base rather than serving it as MoL adapter. The two MoL-served variants share the same architectural pattern: frozen base, small set of LoRA specialists, Proxy-mediated route hop whose label is emitted by L0, and harness that stays close to production during both training and serving. Macaron-V1-Coding-Venti is the single-specialist exception. Contributions. This report describes Macaron-V1 as co-designed system. Concretely, we contribute: Mixture of LoRA architecture. Proxy-mediated, per-turn composition scheme on top of frozen base. The separation makes it possible to add LoRA specialists without retraining the base and to register specialists from different teams or users on one runtime. The shipped Macaron-V1-Venti model instantiates this architecture with four specialists; we report its routing functionality and serving cost, while continual improvement across generations and complementary gains from independently trained specialists remain evaluation targets described in Section 7.3. We release the serving harness at MindLab-Research/Mixtureof-LoRA-Harness (Mind Lab, 2026d). ModelHarness Co-design and RSI. We treat the harness as first-class optimization target: UI4A (Zhuang et al., 2026) is component-native harness for Generative UI, extending our prior schema-native work (Kong et al., 2026; A2UI Project, 2025); our REPL-based agent harness (Wu et al., 2026) treats executable composition and validated reuse as the interface between the model and its tools; and the Harness Context Protocol makes runtime selection, tools, skills, prompts, hooks, sessions, and workspace resources portable and auditable. MindForge, our agentic RL framework, runs three-stage loop of task discovery, trajectory expansion, and linked model/configuration updates against that harness. The experiment reported here isolates only the Expansion stage: the model remains frozen and no optimizer step is taken. In this fixedmodel harness-search study, adaptive search reaches cumulative coverage of 122/122 selected base-failure tasks, while the stronger of two full-set single-configuration sweeps reaches 11/122 (Section 3.2.5). Because task targeting and error rates differ across phases, this result measures configuration-search coverage, not improvement produced by the full RSI training cycle. R3 rollout routing replay (Chiang et al., 2026a; Ma et al., 2025), DSA integration fixes (Chiang et al., 2026b), and IcePop-style token masking (Ling Team, 2025) address rolloutlearner mismatch on the sparse base. Infrastructure. We provide the MinT post-training platform (Lu et al., 2026), including adapter-revision handoff, measured million-entry addressable catalog, and trillion-parameter-class model-parallel paths, together with LongStraw (Zhou et al., 2026a), an architecture-aware response-only execution stack with reported multi-million-token operating points under fixed GPU inventories. These measurements come from the companion systems reports rather than matched Macaron-V1 training runs. Personal Intelligence benchmarks. We introduce Macaron ChatBench, which evaluates context-conditioned agent conversation, and Macaron LivingBench, which evaluates stateful simulated personal-life assistance under evolving conditions. Both evaluate interaction trajectories rather than isolated answers. Evaluation. We evaluate Macaron-V1 across Personal Intelligence (Macaron ChatBench, Macaron LivingBench), agent, coding, and GenUI tracks against six comparison models. We distinguish scores reproduced in our harness from values taken from public reports, and treat the internal Personal Intelligence results as in-distribution evidence rather than as general-capability comparison (Section 6). Report structure. Section 2 describes collaboration through the MoL architecture, including its mechanisms for specialist composition and its paths toward continual learning and collective intelligence. Section 3 5 describes adaptation through ModelHarness Co-design (UI4A, the REPL harness, and Harness Context Protocol) and the recursive self-improvement loop. Section 4 covers the MinT lifecycle, the LongStraw execution path, and sparse-base mismatch controls. Section 5 introduces the benchmarks we evaluate on, Section 6 reports the results, and Section 7 discusses limitations and the roadmap.

sections.title: 2 Mixture of LoRA
sections.content: Mixture of LoRA (MoL) is the architectural spine of Macaron-V1. Instead of training single monolithic model to cover every capability, we keep large base model frozen and layer small set of specialist LoRA adapters (Hu et al., 2022; Schulman and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025; Zhou et al., 2025b) on top. Adapter composition is orchestrated by serving layer, the MoL Proxy, that treats adapter selection as first-class, observable action per user turn rather than as hidden mixer (Mind Lab, 2026d). This section describes the design principle, the specialists shipped in Macaron-V1-Venti, the routing loop and its measured cost, the per-adapter conversation construction that makes routing cheap, the two-level KV-reuse design and its quality trade-off, and the architectural affordances intended to support separately versioned improvement and cross-owner composition. The reference implementation is open-sourced at MindLab-Research/Mixture-ofLoRA-Harness (Mind Lab, 2026d).

sections.title: 2.1 Design Principle
sections.content: Agent workloads combine tasks with very different chain-of-thought patterns: chat, agentic tool use, coding, and GenUI each ask the model to think in different shape. Joint post-training can create cross-task interference, motivating an architecture that makes specialization explicit (Mind Lab, 2026c). The present release does not include the budget-matched single-LoRA comparison needed to quantify that interference, so we treat it as design motivation rather than an empirical finding of this report. MoL exposes the trade-off explicitly through single rule (Mind Lab, 2026c) (Figure 2): Cluster tasks that share skills and thinking patterns into one LoRA, and keep tasks whose skills diverge sharply in separate LoRAs. Two properties fall out of this rule that support the longer-term continual-learning and collective-intelligence goals: The base is frozen. New capabilities are added by training and registering another adapter rather than by re-training the base. Base weight does not get overwritten by later specialization. Adapters are portable. Because the base is shared, specialist trained by one team, or personalized for one user, can be composed with specialists from another team or user on the same runtime (Mind Lab, 2026b). Section 2.7 returns to these properties.

sections.title: 2.2 Specialists in Macaron-V1-Venti
sections.content: Macaron-V1-Venti ships four release-labeled 1B LoRA specialists on top of frozen 744B GLM-5.2 (Zhipu AI, 2026; GLM-5 Team, 2026) base. The specialists absorb work that was split across five adapters in the Macaron-V1-Preview release; most notably, its OpenClaw specialist has been rolled into the Agent adapter L1 (Mind Lab, 2026c,b). The public Venti adapter configurations use rank 16, LoRA alpha 32, and the same attention/MLP target modules for L0L3. Summing the tensor shapes in the released adapter headers gives 7,688,042,496 stored values per adapter; this is logical stored-tensor count, not an active-per-token count or device-memory measurement. We therefore keep the 748B figure as the release-facing label and use the stored count explicitly when discussing residency below. smaller variant, Macaron-V1-Tall, ships the same four-adapter design on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (Qwen Team, 2026a, 2025) base for local deployment. Its public configurations use rank 64, LoRA alpha 128, and expert-specific target parameters; each adapter contains 3,775,651,840 stored values (L2 is stored in F32), giving approximately 50.1B when added to the nominal 35B base. The two adapter budgets are not directly comparable because the bases expose different target-module and expert structures. 6 L0, Chat. Conversational backbone, instruction following, and model identity. L0 also serves as the routing entry point (Section 2.3). L1, Agent. Long-horizon, heavy tool-use tasks including personal-agent workflows and service integrations. Absorbs the Previews OpenClaw adapter. L2, Coding. Code generation, SWE-style tasks (Jimenez et al., 2024), and terminal use. L3, GenUI. UI4A (Zhuang et al., 2026) rendering and UI-driven action; specialized on TSX (React and SolidJS) with the same output serving other targets through framework-specific renderers. The four adapters are resident in the engine under exactly the names L0L3; L0 is also the routing entry.

sections.title: 2.3 Routing Loop
sections.content: MoL does not train separate router model. Adapter selection is decided per user turn by the entry adapter L0s own reasoning and executed by the MoL Proxy. normal user-message request runs three-stage lifecycle: 1. Route. L0 classifies the incoming request into exactly one canonical adapter label from L0L3 under tight decode budget (24 tokens). The router prompt frames the request as quoted, untrusted text, checks the wrapper families in priority order (generative UI, then code/terminal, then personal-agent/living), and returns single canonical label under constrained-decoding grammar that restricts the output to the four legal labels. If L0 selects itself the request stays on L0; otherwise the Proxy switches to the target adapter. 2. Answer. The chosen specialist responds from its own conversation view (Section 2.4), seeded with crossadapter summaries from prior turns. 3. Summary. The specialist emits short summary of what it just did, capped at 192 output tokens. The Proxy stores this summary server-side and never returns it to the client; it becomes shared context that any adapter can inherit on subsequent turns. Model routing. The route is decided entirely by L0s own reasoning: the entry adapter reads the request and emits canonical adapter label under the constrained-decoding grammar, and that label is taken directly as the route. There is no separate router model and no keyword-based rule library overriding the decision; L0 is the router. This makes the routing decision property of the chat specialists understanding of the request, rather than hand-tuned classifier, and lets routing accuracy improve with the base and the L0 adapter rather than with separate artifact. The benchmark families named in the checked-in prompt are routing examples rather than an exhaustive allowlist; other requests are assigned through the prompts semantic boundaries. We do not report benchmark-specific routing audit for PinchBench or ClawGym. Short-circuits. Tool-result stickiness: when the answer stage ends in tool call, the following tool-result turn is locked to the same adapter, skipping routing and summary entirely. Transactional rollback: the Proxy checkpoints conversation state before each turn and restores it on engine failure or client disconnect, so an undelivered turn never enters conversation history. Runtime architecture. The Proxy is engine-agnostic and may sit directly in front of single engine or behind gateway for multi-worker dispatch. Its only OpenAI-compatible model name is Macaron-V1-Venti; internal base and adapter names remain private. It offers three API surfaces (stateless Chat Completions, stateful Responses, and Anthropic Messages), all driven by the same three-stage core. The design builds on multi-tenant LoRA serving research (Chen et al., 2024; Sheng et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2025a) implemented natively in vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) and SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024). Routing cost. Routing is not free: every user turn adds dedicated routing hop and summary hop on top of the specialists own generation. We measure this cost directly on the Macaron-V1-Venti and Macaron-V1Tall Proxies with per-hop timing instrumentation, over multi-turn mixed-domain conversations (48 requests, temperature 0). sections.title:
2.4 Per-Adapter Conversation Views
The central serving-time construction is the own-view : for each engine hop, the Proxy rebuilds the message
list the target LoRA sees, deterministically, from an append-only conversation timeline. Each specialist’s
own past turns are kept verbatim: the full assistant trace, tool calls, and tool results, while every other
specialist’s past turns are collapsed to a single assistant message carrying that turn’s 192-token summary;
the current user turn is appended verbatim. A specialist therefore sees its own raw reasoning history and a
compressed record of what other specialists did, never another specialist’s full trace. Continuity is preserved
without leaking any specialist’s private state.
sections.content: The own-view is what makes routing cheap. Because the timeline is append-only and every own-view is rendered deterministically, re-entering LoRA on later turn produces byte-identical prefix to the previous visit. The engines native, LoRA-aware prefix cache hits on that prefix and only the newly appended tail is prefilled. Per-adapter KV reuse is thus an emergent property of stable per-adapter prompts; it requires no engine modification on this path, and the Proxy surfaces the hit ratio back to the client as prompt-cache metadata for observability. The own-view is served from two state models behind one interface: Proxyauthoritative timeline for the stateful Responses API (the agent sends only the current input and response id), and stateless side-context rebuilt from the agent-resent history for Chat Completions. Routing is query-only and identical on both; only the own-view reconstruction differs. Own-view correctness. The own-view is load-bearing, so we test the paths that depend on it. The multi-hop switching diagnostic of Section 2.3 exercises specialist re-entry after another specialist has run; its aggregate labels verify route re-selection in that smoke test but do not directly measure the semantic fidelity of the reconstructed view. The five-seed Vita result (Table 3: 0.636 direct, 0.650 routed KV-off, 0.632 routed KV-on) shows no detected quality loss from summary-based continuity at this scale. Without paired task-level equivalence analysis, it does not establish identical quality.

sections.title: 2.5 KV Cache Reuse
sections.content: KV reuse in MoL operates at two layers. Emergent reuse via stable own-views (production path, no patch). As described in Section 2.4, the Proxy rebuilds each specialists own-view so that re-entry yields byte-identical prefix, letting the engines native prefix cache absorb the reused portion. Cross-adapter continuity is carried by the 192-token summaries stitched into the own-view; the summary scaffold is never fed into any own-view, so it cannot pollute reusable prefix. This is the default production path and needs no modification to vLLM or SGLang. Same-request route-decode overlay (experimental). When L0 prefills the router prompt and then hands the same request to the target specialist, non-invasive overlay trims the router-only tokens and continues decoding under the selected LoRA, reusing the continuous prefix the two share. On vLLM this is realized through the streaming-input session path: the request is issued as two segments, router segment 9 under L0, then decode segment under the selected LoRA carrying metadata that pins the shared prefix length, so the engine reuses the overlap and prefills only the divergence. On SGLang the same contract is realized by runtime monkey-patch over the scheduler and serving classes. cross-turn flag additionally lets the decode segment read and write the global prefix cache, so later turn on the same adapter can hit this turns prefix. The overlay is one instance of the broader family of low-rank inference shortcuts (Zhou et al., 2026b) that trade small quality margin for decode-speed gain. Boundary. Both layers reuse continuous prefix only. We do not implement arbitrary non-contiguous GPU KV splicing across adapters: specialist switch still invalidates the adapter-specific portion of the KV cache, and the shared prefix is reused only where it is contiguous. The route-decode overlay is an opt-in experimental path; the default deployment runs on the emergent path with unmodified engines. KV-reuse quality trade-off. KV reuse buys latency at potential cost in quality, because reused prefix carries forward prior turns state rather than re-deriving it from the current context. The three-arm Vita sweep of Table 3 isolates this on the emergent path (Layer A): routed reuse-on (0.632 0.019) and routed reuse-off (0.650 0.030) show no detected difference at this scale. The route-decode overlay of Layer is evaluated only in legacy GLM-5.1 shim diagnostic (30 turns, both arms 100% accurate), where per-turn wall time is slightly higher with reuse on because of prefix-trim overhead; this is functionality check, not current-model quality estimate.

sections.title: 2.6 MoL Deployment
sections.content: The deployment study asks systems question distinct from the quality results above: what is the cost of representing several specialists as adapters on one shared model rather than as several independently deployed models? We compare the MoL representation with replicated-base layout in which each of the four LoRA specialists is merged into separate copy of the base. MoL instead keeps one base resident and exposes the specialists as runtime adapters. The two layouts therefore share the same capability partition at the interface level, while differing in parameter sharing and request scheduling. Detailed profiles and measurements are collected in Appendix C. Weight residency and capacity. For the Macaron-V1-Venti configuration, the public adapter headers contain 7,688,042,496 stored values in each of the four LoRA updates. MoL therefore stores one nominal 744B base plus about 30.8B adapter values (approximately 774.8B logical parameters), while the replicated-base layout stores four merged copies of the base (2.976T parameters). On this logical count, MoL is about 26.0% of the replicated layout, 74.0% reduction in stored parameter values. The release-facing 748B label is not used for this residency calculation, because it does not equal the stored tensor count. This is structural consequence of sharing the base and is independent of the attention backend or parallelism layout. In the measured MoL deployments, the remaining device memory supports KV cache and concurrency: H20 sustains sixteen concurrent 56K-token requests, eight 180K-token requests, or four 230K-token requests, while B300 DCP2, DCP4, and DCP8 with EAGLE enabled provide approximately 2.34M, 4.67M, and 9.34M logical KV tokens, respectively. Long-context execution. The long-context path combines page-level context parallelism for prefill, decode context parallelism for KV capacity, and prefilldecode disaggregation. On eight B300 GPUs, CP8 LayerSplit reduces cold needle-test TTFT at 900K tokens from 107.1 to 49.2 while preserving the sparse attention indexers address domain. With DCP8 and EAGLE, the deployment reaches 8.6 ms mean TPOT and 110 tokens/s output throughput at concurrency 1, and 18.0 ms mean TPOT and 757 tokens/s at concurrency 16, without output corruption in the reported stress tests. The EAGLE-enabled path reserves part of the available KV capacity for its draft model and cache. Supporting capacity and latency measurements are reported in Appendix C. Correctness and evidence boundary. Serving efficiency depends on the joint choice of engine, attention backend, parallelism layout, speculative decoding, and request load. We therefore report only measurements whose operating points are sufficiently specified, rather than ranking heterogeneous validation snapshots. In 10 the backend study, FlashMLA sparse attention produced clean outputs for all 48 tested long-context configurations on each of GLM-5.1 and GLM-5.2, whereas the default DSA decode path produced clean outputs in only 6 of 48 GLM-5.1 configurations. Replicated DCP layouts also passed their reported correctness checks, while the sharded DCP path exhibited systematic corruption. These observations determine the validated deployment envelope; they are not cross-engine throughput comparison. Prefilldecode disaggregation remains part of the production profile, but heterogeneous PD snapshots are excluded from the quantitative comparison because they differ in engine, load, LoRA residency, and speculative decoding configuration. These results establish the principal systems advantage of MoL over the replicated-base layout: it removes replicated base-weight residency and makes multi-specialist, long-context service feasible. They do not establish lower TTFT or higher throughput than independently deployed merged specialists; accordingly, we make no comparative latency or throughput claim for that deployment alternative.

sections.title: 2.7 Continual Learning and Collective Intelligence
sections.content: A frozen base plus plug-in adapter registry provides an implementation substrate for separately versioned specialists and, in principle, cross-owner composition (Mind Lab, 2026b; Lu et al., 2026). These are architectural properties, not evidence of improvement across generations or capability gains from specialist population. Three properties follow directly: Adapter registration. new LoRA can be trained and registered without retraining already deployed weights. Whether it improves the intended capability while preserving end-to-end behavior still requires evaluation. Base-weight immutability. Because gradients only enter adapters, the base weights cannot drift as side effect of specialization. This does not guarantee retained system behavior when adapters, routing, or the harness change. Live harness updates. The harness layer (routing rules, tool exposure, HCP configs; see Section 3.1) can be edited without redeploying weights. New tasks become tractable through harness change first, and only get baked into an adapter once the trajectory data is worth training on. This decouples the release cadence of the base, of specialists, and of the harness: each moves on its own clock. Because the base is shared and adapters are portable, the registry can admit specialists trained by different teams or personalized for different users, subject to compatibility and trust checks. The current release evaluates only the four shipped specialists and does not test cross-owner population. Two intended directions follow: Multi-team composition. team could ship specialist targeting domain we do not cover in-house, with the router registry deciding when to hand off. Such release would require compatibility, provenance, and tool-visibility checks that are outside the present evaluation. Personalization at the adapter layer. user-specific adapter could be mounted alongside the shipping specialists. MinTs million-entry adapter catalog (Lu et al., 2026) supplies the addressing mechanism, but this release does not evaluate personalized-adapter quality, privacy, or cross-user composition. We view MoL less as way to make one model bigger and more as an interoperability contract for composable agent capability.

sections.title:
2.8 Discussion
MoL is a bet on orchestration over merging. We do not merge adapter weights into a single forward pass,
and we do not stack them additively. Composition happens at the request level via the routing loop, and
continuity happens via short summaries retained server-side plus the deterministic own-view that makes
per-adapter prefix reuse emerge for free. In the 48-request timing profile, the routing and summary hops
average 0.54 s and 0.97 s, together ∼ 32% of the three-hop total. The router reaches 99.12% on its trace,
while the small Vita comparison detects no reuse-related degradation (reuse-on 0.632 ± 0.019 versus reuse-off
0.650 ± 0.030). Three practical consequences follow: (i) logs attribute each answer to one selected specialist;
(ii) adapter-specific updates leave other adapter weights unchanged, although routing and harness changes
sections.content: 11 can still affect end-to-end behavior; and (iii) new composition patterns can be implemented in the harness without merging adapter weights (Section 3.1). Further KV reuse. The current reuse design reuses L0s KV for the routing portion of each turn, and otherwise lets each specialist reuse only its own prefix. more ambitious design, which we have sketched but not yet shipped, would let every specialist reuse L0s full KV across the board. Because the own-view already reconstructs each specialists context from the shared conversation timeline, L0s KV is natural shared substrate: routing it to every specialist would remove the need for each specialist to carry its own copy of the other specialists summaries, trading the per-adapter summary redundancy for single shared prefix. We do not commit to this design here; it raises correctness questions about mixing chat-adapters KV with specialists own computation, but it is the direction in which the own-view architecture most naturally extends. Single-input multi-intent requests. The routing loop assumes one intent per user turn: it routes the whole turn to one specialist. In practice user often packs several intents into one message: discuss life task, then request code, then ask for UI to show it, and the production system handles this by routing to single specialist and letting the conversation naturally segment over subsequent turns. This is deliberate simplification, not the ceiling of the design. The general case calls for an orchestrator or planner that decomposes multi-intent turn into sequence of specialist sub-tasks and composes their outputs, and we have an exploratory branch that implements this style of decomposition. It is not yet in production: we are designing more uniform and maintainable formulation before shipping it. We report the exploration here as evidence that the architecture admits this extension, and as the direction in which the per-turn routing loop generalizes.

sections.title: 3 Algorithm: Model–Harness Co-design and Recursive Self-Improvement
sections.content: An LLM agent emits text; harness turns that text into actions (Wu et al., 2026). Everything visible to the user, what tools exist, how UI renders, how tool result is fed back into the model, lives in this layer. In Macaron-V1 the harness is first-class training target: we treat trainserve harness divergence as bug to fix at the source rather than as modeling problem to paper over (Mind Lab, 2026c). The harness defines the action interface and the runtime contract the model is trained against; the recursive self-improvement loop then optimizes the modelharness pair over that contract. This section describes the two halves together: first the harness components, then the RSI cycle that runs against them.

sections.title:
3.1 Model–Harness Co-design
A harness is the substrate that determines how much of an agent’s computation can be executed rather than
re-described (Wu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2024). Discrete substrates like one-JSON-tool-per-turn (Patil et al.,
2025) force every intermediate value back through the model as text; expressive substrates keep computation
in a state the model never restates. Holding model, tasks, primitives, and budgets fixed, changing only the
substrate changes both success rate and token cost, sometimes by large factors (Wu et al., 2026).
sections.content: Two design commitments follow from this observation and shape everything in this subsection: The harness should get lighter as the model gets stronger. brittle schema that carries the model is ceiling. harness that expresses ordinary programmer-shaped code lets general model do most of the work, and reserves specialist adapters for judgment calls (Zhuang et al., 2026). Training and serving share an explicit runtime contract. MindForge (Section 3.2) records the HCP and action substrate used by an evaluation backend. Reusing those artifacts makes configuration drift visible; the backend remains responsible for reproducing the production tool surface. 3.1.1 UI4A: Component-Native Harness for Generative UI Generative UI (Leviathan et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025) has historically been approached in two ways, each with ceiling (Figure 3). Figure 3 Three approaches to generative UI. HTML-native maximizes expressiveness but inherits raw web developments failure modes; schema-native is verifiable but capped by the component catalog; UI4A (component-native) lets the model write ordinary frontend code under runtime-enforced boundaries, recovering expressiveness without the schema ceiling. HTML-native. Maximum expressiveness, minimum control (Si et al., 2025); the harness inherits every compiler, bundler, and error-recovery problem of raw web development. Schema-native. Verifiable and auditable but capped by the catalog (A2UI Project, 2025; Kong et al., 2026). The schemas ceiling caps the models ceiling. Our prior schema-native work (Macaron-A2UI (Kong et al., 2026)) taught us the point that most affects shipping agent: teaching the model when to render UI matters more than teaching it how. UI4A (Zhuang et al., 2026) is Macaron-V1s component-native answer. The agent writes ordinary frontend code with imports, components, state, and functions, inside runtime-enforced boundaries. Its mental model is import + component + state + Action: Import. The agent pulls components from curated Macaron registry or common ecosystem primitives (Radix, shadcn, Recharts, KaTeX, lucide-react), with raw HTML/CSS available when case demands it. Component and state. Ordinary frontend code the model already knows how to write; no proprietary schema envelope. Action contract. Every user gesture is structured object with four fields: Origin (which surface), State (what data it read), Execution (local function or agent event), and Visibility (including NoAI boundary for fields the model must not see). The runtime decides whether to run locally, prompt the user, or dispatch as an agent event. Two axes of flexibility follow. The agent can scale down to the curated registry for efficiency, or scale up to arbitrary frontend code (LaTeX, 3D, generative visuals) when the case genuinely requires it (Zhuang et al., 2026). Rendering is framework-agnostic: React, Vue, Svelte, and SolidJS render from the same output; adding target ships small renderer rather than changing the protocol. Because the code the model produces looks like what frontend engineer would already write, the base model handles most of the work. Macaron-V1-Ventis L3 adapter (Section 2.2) specializes in when to render and in picking and binding components correctly. Adapter routing is optional: when the host model does not support adapters, the harness runs against the base at higher token cost and latency. On 48-case internal gallery we measure raw HTML at 1,224 output tokens versus UI4A at 672, 45% reduction (Zhuang et al., 2026); combined with non-reasoning LoRA, streaming, and partial rendering, we observe up to 6 faster time-to-first-render on interactive cases. 13 Figure 4 slice of the UI4A-Bench gallery. Each card is generated as ordinary frontend code under runtime-enforced boundaries; UI4A-Bench scores them on compile/render correctness, control wiring, and screen fit. The L3 specialist decides when to render; the substrate carries how. 3.1.2 REPL Agent Harness: Executable Composition and Validated Reuse Agent workloads lean on the substrate harder than UI does: most of an agents work is intermediate values handed between tool calls, and the substrate decides whether they stay resident in the runtime or return through the model as text. Our agent harness is REPL (Wu et al., 2026), meaning stateful readevalprint loop rather than new agent category: persistent Python namespace, one rung above discrete function calling (Patil et al., 2025), MCP endpoints (Anthropic, 2024), and shell commands. It is the action surface behind the L1 Agent specialist (Section 2.2). The first mechanism is executable composition: dependent values persist as variables, so chain of dependent operations resolves inside single turn, and the model never restates an intermediate it has already computed (Figure 5). Discrete substrates instead pay round-trip per dependency step (Wu et al., 2026); Section 6.3 illustrates the resulting turn and token gap on Macaron-V1-Venti. The second mechanism is validated reuse, which extends composition across tasks. Two operations govern helpers lifecycle: save_tool stages self-derived helper into candidate pool, and promote_tool makes it callable by later queries, but only after it passes private validation run against held-out reference. Promotion after validation is the load-bearing ordering: promoted helper is shared across users later sessions and is live in MindForge rollouts (Section 3.2.2), so promoting one unvalidated would turn one-off local error into standing fault across both serving and training. promotion that later proves bad is logged and demoted, not silently retained. 14 Figure 5 Executable composition. Under function calling (left), each intermediate observation returns through the model as text: one round-trip per dependency step. In the REPL (right), dependent values persist in executable state (orders, net), so the same chain resolves in single round-trip. Arrow thickness is observation size. Because promotion is scoped, users recurring workflow compiles into validated helper in their own namespace, captured without gradient step. External services enter the namespace through ToolProxy: Python-shaped wrappers carrying NoAI visibility boundaries and retry semantics, so that model-facing signature matches runtime behavior by construction, the tool-exposure contract of Section 3.1.3 (Mind Lab, 2026b). MindForge imports this same harness object rather than stand-in, which forecloses trainserve tool drift at the source. The REPL is not universally best: stateful observe-before-commit APIs (Patil et al., 2025) penalize committing several dependent calls blind, and independent shell tasks (TerminalBench Authors, 2026) give it nothing to compose; there the harness lets the L1 agent fall back to shell or discrete calls. 3.1.3 Harness Context Protocol Real-world agent runs depend on configuration that is otherwise scattered across command-line flags, environment setup, local files, and runtime-specific defaults. The Harness Context Protocol (HCP) is versioned TOML contract for recreating that runtime from portable, auditable artifact (Mind Lab, 2026a). Its purpose is narrower and more operational than generic context configuration: an HCP producer writes run specification, and consumer resolves it in deterministic order before creating the agent session. The concrete surface HCP standardizes: Runtime and model selection. Working directory, backend, provider, model identifier, context window, generation limits, and provider options. Action surface. Tool allowlists, MCP servers, extensions, hooks, and the policies that control what the agent may invoke. Context resources. System prompts, AGENTS.md-style files, skills, prompt templates, embedded resources, and their deterministic materialization. Session and workspace state. Session snapshots plus optional workspace inputs, visibility, snapshot policy, and declared outputs. 15 Environment contract. Required and optional environment names, path-resolution rules, and secret references without embedding portable credentials. The current Python SDK operates in wrapper mode: it validates the outer configuration, asks pi-hcp to prepare the runtime, launches the ACP process, and manages session through the Agent Client Protocol (Mind Lab, 2026a). Full semantic validation and native Python materialization remain outside the SDK. In the RSI loop, HCP therefore serves as the versioned boundary between configuration search and execution. It is worth being precise about what is and is not trainable here, because the two are easy to conflate. The protocol carries no gradients: an HCP artifact is declarative TOML document, and no optimizer ever writes to it. What the model can do is rewrite the harness the protocol describes. Because prompts, skills, tool allowlists, hooks, and workspace resources are all addressable fields in portable artifact, model version can propose edits to them, have the edits evaluated on re-run of the affected slice, and ship the survivors as the next configuration, self-iteration of the harness conducted in language space rather than in parameter space (Section 3.2.3). Neither half is sufficient alone. Configuration search moves in discrete jumps and cannot acquire skill the base does not already have, though Section 3.2.5 measures how much of what scores as missing skill is an unelicited one; adapter training acquires skills but cannot reach the tool surface or the instructions that decide when to use them. Coupled through MinT, which parameterizes the specialists as LoRA revisions over frozen base (Section 4.1) (Lu et al., 2026), the pair becomes one trainable system: candidate HCP is what rollout executes against, the resulting trajectories are what the adapters are trained on, and MindForge ships the two as linked modelconfiguration version. The trainable object is the modelharness pair, not the protocol. 3.1.4 Live Harness Updates Enable Continual Learning Section 2.7 described the frozen base and adapter registry as an architectural affordance for continual learning. The harness supplies the operational revision path: new capability may first appear as registered tool, HCP configuration, UI4A component, or REPL helper promoted after validation. When trajectory evidence warrants parameter update, the change can then be transferred into specialist adapter. The present evaluation measures the configuration-search stage, not repeated transfer across adapter generations. This gives Macaron-V1 three release clocks: the base (tied to platform-level models such as GLM-5.2 (Zhipu AI, 2026; GLM-5 Team, 2026)), the specialists (updated through the RSI process in Section 3.2), and the harness. Harness changes do not require weight update, so they can be evaluated and released on shorter cycle than new base or specialist revision.

sections.title: 3.2 Recursive Self-Improvement
sections.content: Macaron-V1 is improved through versioned data-generation and training cycle rather than fixed posttraining corpus. The cycle runs against the production harness described above: model version proposes tasks beyond its current competence, attempts them in an executable agent environment, and produces evaluated trajectories. Those trajectories support two different forms of improvement: language-space search over the runtime configuration, and parameter updates to the specialist adapters. MindForge maintains the lineage connecting problem banks, evaluation runs, selected trajectories, training jobs, configurations, and model versions. This subsection describes the optimization object, the role of the framework, and the recursive self-improvement (RSI) cycle that connects them (Figure 6). 3.2.1 Agent RL on Frozen Sparse Base Let θ denote the parameters of the frozen sparse base, ϕ the trainable LoRA parameters, and versioned harness configuration. The agent policy can be written as where ot contains the conversation and observations exposed by the harness, and at is model-visible action. An action may be message, clarification, discrete tool call, or an expression evaluated by the stateful πϕ(at ot; θ, c), (1) 16 Figure 6 The three loops that share one harness. MindForge runs RL rollouts against the same agent harness used for production serving; an HCP contract serializes the harness context (router, memory, resources, prompts, and tool-call tokens) so training and serving configurations can be compared explicitly. Matching the recorded contract makes configuration drift auditable but does not guarantee behaviorally identical executions. readevalprint loop defined in Section 3.1.2. Adapter selection is separate Proxy-mediated route hop (Section 2.3), not tool call made from this action space. The resulting episode is recorded as τ = (o0, a0, . . . , oT , aT , y), (2) where contains the task-level outcome and any process-level judgments attached by the evaluator. This factorization distinguishes two update paths that are easy to conflate. Model optimization changes ϕ while keeping θ fixed; configuration search selects new without treating HCP as learned parameter. The training backend uses GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) to update the adapters from selected trajectories. Sparsebase rollout consistency and long-context execution are handled by the infrastructure in Section 4. This release reports the adapter training configuration (learning rate, batch size, epochs, schedule, and optimizer) in Appendix B.6. The action substrate is part of c, not an incidental wrapper. In the REPL substrate, dependent primitive operations execute inside persistent namespace, so intermediate values need not be serialized through the model after every call (Wu et al., 2026). For stateful APIs that require observing one result before committing the next action, the same runtime can instead expose discrete calls. The policy is therefore trained and evaluated against an explicit action interface rather than an abstract tool-use label. 3.2.2 MindForge: Lifecycle Orchestration MindForge is the control plane of the RSI cycle. It manages problem banks, evaluation runs, conversion of evaluated trajectories into trainable datasets, training jobs, and version registry that links each model to its parent, data, configuration, and evaluation results. Compute-heavy operations are delegated through pluggable benchmark and training backends. The control plane consequently defines lifecycle and provenance, while backend defines the semantics of task execution, scoring, and optimization. An HCP artifact provides the backend with versioned runtime contract (Section 3.1.3) (Mind Lab, 2026a). It records model and provider selection, tool policy, skills, prompts, MCP servers, hooks, session state, and workspace staging. The selected action substrate determines how model outputs become executable actions. 17 Recording both artifacts makes run reconstructable at the configuration boundary: trainserve differences can be inspected as differences in configuration, resources, or backend realization. This is reproducibility contract, not claim that two executions are behaviorally identical. After each update, MinT exports the changed LoRA state as serving-compatible adapter revision instead of moving or merging the frozen base; trajectories, rewards, and routing metadata remain separate rollout records (Section 4.1) (Lu et al., 2026). This separation also keeps framework claims aligned with implementation. MindForge does not redefine GRPO, the REPL, or HCP. It connects their artifacts into stable lineage: (problem bank, model, HCP) evaluated trajectories (dataset, next model, next HCP). The lineage is the unit of an RSI generation. model checkpoint without its problem-bank version, selected data, and runtime configuration is an incomplete record of the experiment. 3.2.3 Three-Stage RSI Cycle Discovery. Starting from versioned seed bank, the current model proposes harder task variants by lifting constraints, introducing hidden preferences, chaining sub-goals, or embedding contradictions. Each proposal must include either verifiable answer or an evaluation rubric. Candidate tasks are retained only when they satisfy two complementary criteria: quality, meaning that the task and its evaluation are well-defined, and learning value, meaning that the current model does not already solve the task reliably. The verifier, difficulty estimator, and acceptance thresholds belong to the benchmark backend; MindForge records the resulting bank and its provenance. Expansion. The accepted tasks are executed by the current model under fixed modelHCP pair. The evaluator scores both task outcome and relevant process behavior, producing set of trajectories rather than single answer corpus. Audits then localize failure to the model, the task, or the harness configuration. For example, an audit may reveal unnecessary model round-trips, an action that should have remained discrete, missing tool boundary, or an instruction that causes premature routing. Candidate changes to prompts, skills, tool exposure, hooks, and other HCP-carried resources are evaluated by re-running the affected slice. Section 3.2.5 reports what this search recovers on set the base fails outright. Configuration changes are accepted on observed behavior rather than on prompt-author intuition; the acceptance gate is an automatic eval pass against the affected benchmark slice, with human review reserved for changes that touch tool exposure or safety-relevant boundaries. Update. Trajectory selection filters invalid runs, removes duplicates, and retains examples that are both validated and informative for the next model. The selected trajectories become input to the training backend, which updates the LoRA specialists while the sparse base remains frozen. In parallel, the accepted HCP is registered as the runtime configuration of the next generation. MindForge links the new adapter state and HCP to their parent artifacts and evaluation evidence. The resulting modelconfiguration pair returns to discovery, where its changed competence induces new task distribution. The three stages therefore form feedback system. Discovery adapts the curriculum to the current policy; expansion searches behavior in the executable environment; update transfers validated behavior into parameters while preserving the configuration that produced it. Progress is measured across linked generations, not inferred from the existence of later checkpoint. 3.2.4 AutoResearch, Trajectory Selection, and Context Learning The Preview report (Mind Lab, 2026c) described self-evolution through AutoResearch, trajectory selection, In V1 these and what it called context learning (validated-trajectory transfer, not in-context learning). mechanisms are integrated into the three-stage cycle above. AutoResearch is language-space search inside expansion. The model proposes changes to prompts, skills, scaffolds, or tool-use policy; when represented by HCP resources, each proposal becomes portable candidate 18 Table 4 Phase breakdown of the 69-job expansion run of Figure 7. Attempts count task trials, so job sweeping the full set contributes 122. Pooled rate is passes over attempts within the phase; coverage is the cumulative unique tasks passed at the end of it, against the fixed denominator of 122. The model is frozen throughout. Trajectory selection closes expansion by deciding which observed behaviors should influence the next model. useful trajectory is not merely successful: it must be valid under the evaluator, attributable to the intended task and configuration, and sufficiently informative to justify inclusion. This selection step prevents configuration search, evaluator failures, and duplicated solutions from being indiscriminately distilled into the model. Context learning is the transfer from validated language-space behavior to the parameter update. Selected trajectories provide the training signal for the next adapters, while the accepted HCP remains separately versioned artifact. Keeping these outputs distinct makes it possible to ask whether gain came from weights, configuration, or their interaction. This release does not report that quantitative attribution; the controlled generation-by-generation comparison that would isolate it remains required. 3.2.5 Expansion Coverage on Base-Failure Set The expansion stage searches configuration space against fixed task set. We measure its reach on 122 simulation tasks grouped under 29 TerminalBench 2.1 (TerminalBench Authors, 2026) source families, selected precisely because the frozen GLM-5.2-FP8 base scores every one of them not-pass under the official reward. sections.title: 4 Infrastructure
sections.content: The RSI cycle in Section 3.2 links new LoRA adapter revision to the HCP configuration, selected data, and evaluation artifacts that produced it. This section concerns the model-state side of that lineage and the computation that produces the revision. MinT manages the model-state lifecycle over resident, frozen base; LongStraw provides response-only execution path when an update has very long context; and modeldependent controls limit rollouttraining mismatch on sparse bases. These components do not change the learned unit defined earlier: the deployable model update remains an exported LoRA revision, paired by MindForge with the HCP and evaluation artifacts that produced it. Figure 8 separates lifecycle management from the optional, architecture-specific execution mechanisms inside an update. deployed interactions Production harness HCP + tools MindForge experience loop MinT managed update/export Adapter revision versioned LoRA MoL serving specialist composition Conditional update mechanisms LongStraw response-only replay Sparse-base controls R3 + DSA alignment + filtering Figure 8 Infrastructure inside the Macaron revision loop. This is conceptual artifact and control flow, not claim that all components are co-located or invoked for every update. MindForge supplies selected trajectories and identifies the current policy; MinT resolves its policy record, manages the update, and exports an immutable LoRA adapter revision for the MoL runtime. LongStraw is selected for long-context response-only updates; sparse-base consistency controls are selected according to the model architecture. The dashed feedback arrow denotes experience collected after deployment, not an automatic online weight update (Lu et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026a).

sections.title:
4.1 MinT: Model-State Lineage over a Resident Base
The MindLab Toolkit (MinT) (Lu et al., 2026) manages LoRA RL over resident dense and Mixture-of-Experts
(MoE) base deployments. Its key distinction is between an adapter revision, an immutable LoRA snapshot
exported at a particular training step in serving tensor layout, and a policy record, the mutable service state
used to resume and audit that policy. The policy record names the compatible base version and adapter
shape, the latest trainer checkpoint and optimizer state, associated rollout records, and the available exported
revisions. Training restores mutable state on a compatible worker, whereas rollout, evaluation, and serving
select an exported revision; trainer checkpoints and optimizer state never cross the serving boundary directly.
sections.content: This abstraction provides model-state lineage, not complete experimental reproducibility by itself. Prompts, tools, hooks, workspace resources, task-bank versions, evaluators, and sampling settings remain in the HCP and MindForge artifacts defined in Section 3.2.2. reported run is therefore reconstructable at the papers configuration boundary only when its adapter revision and compatible base are joined with those artifacts. The narrower MinT guarantee is that rollout or score can be attributed to fixed adapter revision even if trainer placement and serving-cache residency change. The companion MinT experiment compares merge path that materializes and loads full checkpoint before its rollout probe with an adapter path that loads the exported revision into sampler whose base is already resident. Under those stated probes, adapter-only handoff reduces the measured handoff step by 18.3 for Qwen3-4B with rank-32 adapter and by 2.85 for Qwen3-30B with rank-16 adapter (Lu et al., 2026). Serving experiments select bounded working sets from that catalog while each actor maintains smaller CPU cache and GPU-active window (Lu et al., 2026). Thus, 106 is measured artifact-addressability result. It does not mean that one engine holds one million adapters in GPU memory, nor that the entries represent one million independently trained or behaviorally distinct policies. Cold loading remains scheduled service work, and revision becomes uservisible only after compatibility checking and activation. This is the catalog boundary assumed by the registry in Section 2.7 (Chen et al., 2024; Sheng et al., 2023). The companion report includes Kimi K2 countdown-task LoRA RL run on 1.04T-total/32.6B-active parameter base using 64 H800 GPUs (Lu et al., 2026; Moonshot AI, 2025). This is evidence that the adapter lifecycle executes on that model and workload; it is not evidence that Macaron-V1 was trained on Kimi K2, nor that the run is reproducible from this paper alone.
